producer: Distillerie de la Salers (Distillerie des Terres Rouges)
title: Salers Gentiane Aperitif
about: Salers is the oldest of the surviving gentian-liqueur houses. Alfred Labounoux founded it in 1885 at Montaignac-Saint-Hippolyte in the Corrèze, and named it after the Auvergne town of Salers, beneath the Puy Mary, an extinct volcano whose slopes are famed for their yellow gentian. In 2006 the house joined the Védrenne family group and moved to Turenne, near Brive, under the Pagès-Védrenne banner. Its range is sold under the Distillerie des Terres Rouges label, which also covers the house’s fig aperitif, walnut wine, pastis and fruit liqueurs.

The bitterness comes from the root of Gentiana lutea, which the house grows in the open fields of the Auvergne and which takes around twenty years to mature. The roots are dug by hand, then washed and crushed within twenty-four hours and macerated in alcohol for several weeks. The roots are distilled in copper stills and the distillate is married with that first maceration and other botanicals, then aged more than three years in Limousin oak vats, a long rest for the category. Water, neutral alcohol and a little sugar are added before bottling at 16% alcohol.

Salers uses no artificial colouring, so it keeps a natural pale straw colour, and it is less sweet than its larger rivals. Expect an earthy, rustic bitterness with cut grass, citrus peel, mint and anise. The classic French way is on ice with a squeeze of lemon, or with lemonade or soda; it also stands in for Suze in a White Negroni.
